data.title: The Twilight of Great Moravia – a legend from the 10th century
data.excerpt: A legend from the final phase of Great Moravia, set in the summer of 907 at the Priekopa hillfort at Zvolen-Môťová and recorded by Radoslav Mandalík. It is a fictionalised story in a real historical setting: župan Ratihoj answers Prince Mojmír’s call to arms and only a fraction of his men come home.

timeline.title: The last mention of a Great Moravian market
timeline.description: The charter on the Raffelstetten toll mentions the market of the Moravians – one of the last written mentions of Great Moravia.

timeline.title: The defeat of the Magyars by the Moravians
timeline.description: The Moravians still defeated the Magyars, which is the last known military mention of the empire before its demise.

timeline.title: The action of the legend at the hillfort near Zvolen
timeline.description: The legend records the fates of župan Ratihoj and his family at the Priekopa hillfort at Zvolen-Môťová at the time when Prince Mojmír II is calling up the army against the Magyars.

timeline.title: The battle near Bratislava and the demise of Great Moravia
timeline.description: A “very unfortunate” battle took place near Bratislava, in which the Old Hungarians defeated the Bavarians; the Great Moravian army of Mojmír II is no longer mentioned and the central princely power comes to an end.

timeline.title: The battle of the Lech
timeline.description: After the defeat at the Lech near Augsburg the Old Hungarians go over to a settled way of life and settle permanently in the Carpathian Basin.

children.text: A legend from the period of the final phase of Great Moravia, from the beginning of the 10th century, was recorded and published by JUDr. Radoslav Mandalík in his book Historické povesti zo Zvolenskej a Šarišskej stolice (Historical legends from the Zvolen and Šariš counties). With his consent we bring you this exceptional and interesting legend in full. Great thanks are due to the author. It is an author’s fictionalised story set in a real historical environment, not a legend handed down by folk tradition. The author states this in the preface to his collection as well.
THE TWILIGHT OF GREAT MORAVIA
A legend from the beginning of the 10th century

The territory of Zvolen was settled from the earliest times. Its advantageous position and natural endowments provided suitable conditions for occupation as early as prehistory and antiquity. The museum holds valuable finds from the Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages, from the Lusatian culture, from the period of the Celts, as well as artefacts from the Roman period. Slavic occupation from the 6th–7th century onwards is attested by several archaeological finds of Slavic settlements.
Among the important Slavic (Great Moravian) settlements in central Slovakia are the central hillfort of
Priekopa at Zvolen-Môťová
, the hilltop (guard) hillfort at nearby Detva-Kalamárka, which guarded the important road from the Ipeľ region into the Zvolen Basin, and the fortified settlement of Hrádok at Lieskovec.

The Great Moravian period belongs among the most important sections of our earliest history. Several written sources speak of Great Moravia, a strong early feudal state. The last mentions of Great Moravia are from the year 905 (the reference to the market of the Moravians in the charter on the Raffelstetten toll) and from 906 (the defeat of the Magyars by the Moravians).
The legend presented here offers a view of the fates of the people of that time, the inhabitants of one of the hillforts, in the broader context of the demise of Great Moravia.
The summer of 907.
Over the
hillfort at Zvolen
a new day is dawning.

The guards drive away the last remnants of sleep. The crowing of the cockerels wakes the household servants, who after a brief refreshment begin their everyday work. They rake out the hearths, light the fire and prepare breakfast for the župan (the prince’s regional governor), his family and the other inhabitants of the hillfort. Before long the hillfort is as busy and lively as usual. The baker, the butcher and the carpenter set off to work. From the smithy, too, the banging of the hammer on the anvil can soon be heard. The smith shoes horses and makes axes, sickles and knives, but also daggers and swords for the warriors.

Župan Ratihoj receives the report of the commander of the guard, an experienced man who had already served under his father. The steward reports on the state of the stores. In the preceding days the inhabitants of the hamlets had been coming to the hillfort and, as every year, handing over the prescribed princely and župan’s tax. Grain, smoked and salted meat, fish, lard, wax and honey. The Zvolen župan, like his father and his grandfather before him, is a powerful lord of the region. That year the harvest was good, and the granaries and stores at the hillfort are full to the very top.

Together with the commander Tur, the župan walks round the ramparts and checks the completion of the fortification works. The hillfort is well protected by a massive ditch and, from the north, by the river Slatina. The strengthened ramparts with their palisade will hold off even a possible attack by the Magyars. The župan does not hide his satisfaction.

On the open ground below the hillfort young warriors have gathered and are training in the handling of weapons. A small group of older, experienced soldiers watches them. The lads with swords, shields and battle axes attack and defend in turn. Others throw spears and shoot at a target with the bow. The župan and the commander stop beside them for a while. With pleasure they watch the performance of the best – the župan’s eldest son Milota and his most faithful friend, the commander’s son Svatoš. Milota was brought up for a time at the princely court in Nitra. Both were admitted into the military retinue the summer before last. Among the boys, the župan’s younger son Levoslav also does well in shooting with the bow; he only recently underwent the rite of postrižiny, the ceremonial first haircut.
In the afternoon the guard from the tower by the gateway reports the arrival of merchants.

In a moment a small merchant caravan comes in through the gateway of the hillfort. After a brief welcome the merchants unpack and offer their goods in the enclosure. The župan’s wife Slávená, with her daughter, the young Zora, and her companions, look with enthusiasm at the precious fabrics and ornaments from distant lands. The warriors weigh in their hands swords and daggers with decorated hilts, made by masters as far away as Byzantium. In exchange for the goods the merchants ask for good furs, but they will not scorn things from the spoils of war either. The enclosure is busy, here and there laughter and teasing can be heard. Among the people, however, a certain uneasiness can still be felt. Nor do the merchants intend to stay the night. They smile; to questions about whether they have seen foreign warriors on the way they give no answer. They are in a hurry, they say, to further trade in Bohemia and on the Baltic.

Ratihoj returns to the spacious log building that serves as the dwelling of the župan and his family. The hall is decorated with furs, deer antlers and boar tusks. In the middle a large oak table, a stone hearth and the župan’s wooden seat. Clouds darken the župan’s face.
The empire is in danger!

Only a few years ago, after hard fighting with the Germans, Prince Mojmír concluded peace. Now there is a new enemy. The Magyars, nomadic tribes from the east. The frontier units have so far fought hard but successful battles with them. Today, however, the danger is greater than ever before. The Magyars have taken and destroyed several hillforts and hamlets, occupied the Tisza region and Transdanubia and are rolling irresistibly westwards. News of this is brought by refugees who have managed to escape death or slavery. The frontier of the empire has shifted almost as far as the Hron. For that reason they are in constant contact with the neighbouring magnates and chieftains. Ratihoj has the best relations with Rastislav, the chieftain from nearby Kalamárka, with whom he is now also related by marriage. For Ratihoj’s son Milota had fallen for Rastislav’s younger daughter Lada. In the spring they celebrated their wedding. How much roast meat they ate then and how much good mead they drank! Lada is now with child.

The worried župan can hardly hide his fears from those close to him. In his life he had witnessed both joy and misfortune, the glorious victories of Svatopluk, but also the fratricidal struggle of the princes, his sons. He bears responsibility for his people, while his faithful wife Slávená is his support.

His fears were fulfilled. Before long a messenger arrived at the hillfort with a summons for Ratihoj. Prince Mojmír is calling up the army against the enemies. Every magnate, župan and chieftain is obliged to present himself without delay, with as many men as possible, at the assembly point of the princely army in Nitra.

Ratihoj does not wait. As his duty demands, he and the commander hastily put together a detachment. Among the warriors he includes Milota and Svatoš as well. They prepare the armament and supplies for the men and the horses. Only a few soldiers remain at home. The župan entrusts the protection of the hillfort during his absence to the commander Tur. He orders the elders of the hamlets to prepare abatis on the roads and mountain passes. In case of need, let the people be ready to hide in the mountains.

The time of departure comes. Ratihoj and Milota take leave of the family. Lady Slávená with her daughter Zora, and Lada, can only with effort hold back their tears. The younger Levoslav looks with pride at those departing. Svatoš and Zora exchange a brief glance bearing witness to feelings kept hidden. The old commander Tur knows his son well. Apart from him, no one has so far noticed the relationship growing between the young people.

It is clear to everyone that the fate of the empire, that the future, is at stake. Before the gateway, the detachment led by the župan joins the men led by Rastislav and by Miloš, the chieftain from nearby Lieskovec. By agreement, the chieftains’ families will await their return together at Zvolen. Along the way, small groups of men, free inhabitants of the surrounding hamlets, who will go on foot, are to join the detachments.
The armed men vanish into the distance.

For those who stayed at home, the following days pass slowly. The household servants go about their everyday work, the craftsmen produce objects of daily use. The fishermen catch fish. The farmers cart straw from the fields. The shepherds drive the cattle out to pasture. Lady Slávená, together with the old commander, directs life at the hillfort with a firm hand. Together with the families of the chieftains Rastislav and Miloš they pray for the return of the warriors.

Two weeks have passed. There is no news of the princely army. One day a throng of people passes along the highway. Lady Slávená with the commander and two soldiers stop several of them and offer them bread and water. The strangers are coming from a hamlet by the Danube. They are terrified. They say that everything is over. The wild Magyars are said to be flooding the whole region. They are fleeing further north to safety.
The news of the disaster was, alas, soon confirmed.

The guard spotted the return of the warriors. It was not a victorious return. Of the men who had recently set out with Ratihoj, Rastislav and Miloš, only a fraction remained. Almost all are wounded. One has a shoulder injured by an arrow, another a slashed face, a third drags a wounded leg behind him. One of the soldiers leads a horse pulling a hastily made stretcher. On it lies the battered župan Ratihoj. Even unconscious he grips his sword in his hand. Lady Slávená and her daughter run up to the stretcher. They all enter the hillfort. They lay the župan on a bed in the house and cover him with a bearskin. The women take care of the warriors, press food and water on them and tend their inflamed wounds. What they had feared has happened. The warriors bring news of defeat! In the care of his wife and daughter, župan Ratihoj comes round in the evening. Of the once strong man there is now a broken human being. The women are seized by a bad premonition. At last Ratihoj is able to recount what happened. The princely army is defeated! Some of the Nitran and Moravian magnates wilfully failed to present themselves to the army. They met the Magyars in battle south of the Danube. The enemies were in overwhelming strength. On swift horses they attacked from all sides, shot off arrows and then seemed to withdraw again. Some of the commanders disobeyed the prince’s orders. They chased after the enemy, who managed to cut them off. The weakened and divided princely army succumbed. Prince Mojmír, his retinue and the magnates perished. Part of the princely warriors took refuge behind the walls of some old fortress. In a brave fight against overwhelming odds there fell the chieftain Rastislav, the chieftain Miloš, and Milota with Svatoš. Both fought to the very end, protecting each other. Many nomads fell under the blows of their swords. He was unable to prevent it. Only he and a few men managed, by a miracle, to fight their way through and get home by roundabout routes.

After these words those present could not hold back their tears. Rastislav’s and Miloš’s families had lost a father and protector. The župan and Lady Slávená their eldest son and heir. The young Lada was widowed and her unborn child had lost its father. The commander Tur had lost his only son.

Grief reigned at the hillfort. Women and mothers lament the loss of their loved ones. The uncertainty and fear were so great that everyone goes about as if without a soul. On the third day after the warriors’ arrival, in the presence of a priest, they prayed at the cross for the salvation of the souls of the dead, whom they could not even bury. After the funeral ceremony, Rastislav’s and Miloš’s families returned home.
The refugees grow more numerous every day. Some of them have their property loaded on carts, most of them have nothing. Some of the refugees settle near the hillfort, in Budča and nearby Rybáre.

The summer was slowly ending. Despite the misfortune that had befallen them, life had to go on. Župan Ratihoj recovered from his wounds. Together with the commander Tur they made up the garrison of the hillfort with men from the hamlets. According to the reports, the Magyars had ravaged several regions and also the seat city of Velehrad. Some magnates and chieftains had, it was said, submitted to the foreign chiefs.

The autumn work in the fields was finished. They managed to gather enough wood for heating and fodder for the cattle for the winter. The autumn passed too. In December an unusually harsh winter set in. Everything was buried in snow. People hardly left their dwellings. The grief of the inhabitants of the hillfort was overlaid by a joyful event. In the middle of winter, Lada, Milota’s widow, gave birth to a son as sturdy as a beech. At his baptism they gave him his father’s name.
To the old commander Tur the župan gave, for his faithful service, a hamlet not far from Zvolen which to this day is called Turová.

With the birth of his grandson, Ratihoj and his wife Slávená seemed to recover their former joy. No one knows what the future will bring. The younger son Levoslav will soon grow into a handsome and powerful young man, a worthy successor to his father. The župan’s line will live on.

In the year 907 a “very unfortunate” battle took place near Bratislava, in which the Old Hungarians defeated the Bavarians. The Great Moravian army of Mojmír II is no longer mentioned in this connection. In that year Prince Árpád, the founder of the future royal dynasty, died. Sometime in 906–907 a decisive battle between the Mojmírids and the Old Hungarians probably also took place. According to the tradition recorded by the chronicler Simon of Kéza in the 13th century, this may have happened south of Komárno, at Bánhida, in the present-day Republic of Hungary.

The central princely power, and with it Great Moravia, comes to an end. Old Hungarian warbands ravaged part of Great Moravia and continued with plundering expeditions into the East Frankish Empire. In the areas north of the occupied territories, further (post-Great Moravian) development continued. This was also the case in the region of the middle Hron. After the defeat at the Lech near Augsburg in 955, the Old Hungarians go over to a different way of life and settle permanently in the Carpathian Basin. The more northerly and more mountainous regions of Slovakia are gradually incorporated into the new Hungarian state arising on the foundations of the preceding state organisation.

A massive fortification was built at the Priekopa hillfort near Môťová as late as the 10th century. After the demise of the hillfort in the 11th century its function is taken over by a larger centre – the castle of Starý Zvolen.
